Living off the Land

What a legitimate binary can be made to do · abuse functions, offensive tooling and the benign baseline

The hardest adversary to see is the one using the tools already on the host. Nothing is dropped, no signature fires, and every process in the tree is one that belongs there. This dataset is the part of the corpus that addresses that directly: it records what ordinary binaries can be turned into, which of them attackers actually bring with them, and — just as importantly — what those same binaries look like when nothing is wrong.

Abuse functions

The GTFOBins corpus catalogues binaries that ship on a normal system and the functions each can be coerced into performing: a shell where a pager was expected, a file read through a program with no business reading it, a privilege boundary crossed by a helper that was trusted to cross it. Each binary carries its abuse categories and the invocations that demonstrate them, and the invocations are kept whole rather than reduced to the binary name — because which invocation was used is the difference between evidence and coincidence.

Offensive tooling

The second catalogue is tooling an attacker brings: the Kali distribution’s programs, with their documented purpose, categories and flags. Admission is on purpose, not on presence — attacker tooling is carried onto a host, so its absence from a probed image is expected rather than weak evidence, and the usual instinct to admit only what was observed would exclude the entire category. Defensive categories are excluded, and dual-use programs are flagged rather than quietly counted as offensive.

The benign baseline

A catalogue of what a binary can do is a list of suspicions, not detections. The counterweight is a baseline of what ordinary execution actually produces, measured through the same extraction path so it speaks the same vocabulary as everything it is compared against. Without it, presence is mistaken for evidence — and on a normal system most of these binaries are present, most of the time, doing exactly what they are for.

How the three are joined

on evidence A binary is proposed for a technique because the corpus supports it, not because it ranked highly. An early version cut at a fixed rank with a floor that never fired, so every technique returned the same number of programs and one sandbox tool reached over half of them. Rank is a tie-break, never an admission.
whole invocations An abuse function is admitted with the invocation intact. Reduced to a bare program name it would match every ordinary use of that program, which is the failure mode this category exists to avoid.
dual-use kept Programs that are legitimately administrative and legitimately offensive stay marked as both. Collapsing them either way produces a rule that is wrong in one direction on every host.
retrievable A program that is absent from the reference spine can never be proposed at all — retrieval runs over those documents. Widening the spine is what made a whole class of network tooling visible to the correlation in the first place.

What comes out is a set of proposals per technique, each carrying the evidence that admitted it. That is deliberately weaker than a rule and deliberately stronger than a guess: it is the shortlist a detection author starts from, with the reason it was shortlisted attached.
